“Our belief is we are victims of law discrimination,” Xanamane says.
Most were sympathetic but said the couple needed birth certificates.
Xanamane and Cheng were aware from previous experiences of a foreign-born individual needing a birth certificate for a marriage license, yet they had no firsthand knowledge of someone encountering such an issue. There is no place in the law for them to have obtained such a document before they sought it.
So they had only their green card, both for the original marriage and for getting a marriage license.
They reached out to other refugees, who explained the predicament. Pat Xayachack, a community organizer in Baton Rouge who dedicates his days to assisting recent immigrants, said there are thousands of such cases among multiple generations.
Xayachack was married in what he describes as the Louisiana legal system, which requires both a marriage license and a birth certificate.
Two years ago, during the courthouse visit for his sister’s marriage, he was turned away, too, because he was missing a birth certificate.
This summer, individuals born abroad seeking to marry in Louisiana are required to show both an unexpired visa (although a federal court has declared that marriage licenses should not be denied due to immigration status) and, rather strangely, a birth certificate.
No birth certificate, no marriage, no excuses. It seemed to achieve the broad impact that the policy supporters had anticipated: it has de facto banned marriage for thousands.
Those with legal status in the United States have few sources for birth certificates. Even those who never lived in or near a refugee camp say it’s nearly impossible to get documents. In Louisiana, similar to many states, the process of remaking family records following the Holocaust almost a century ago led to scant records of refugees and limited assistance from organizations in tracing their origins.
